chapter.name: Empires and Kingdoms: 6th to 10th Centuries
chapter.blurb: Harsha and Xuanzang, the Tripartite Struggle, Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, Kashmir, Chalukyas, Pallavas, southern kingdoms, polity, economy, society, culture, science and foreign invasions.

scope_in.item: The Tripartite Struggle and the Palas

concepts.name: Harshavardhana and Xuanzang
concepts.description: The rise of Harsha at Kannauj, his literary court, Bana and Xuanzang's travels.
concepts.idea: Harsha ruled north India from Kannauj, and Xuanzang's travelogue is a key source.
concepts.rule: After the Guptas, many regional powers arose. Harshavardhana of the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty ascended the throne in 606 CE at Kannauj; the earlier capital was Sthaneshvara. He expanded his empire over northern and eastern India. A fine poet and dramatist, he is assumed to have written three Sanskrit plays. He patronised Bana, author of Kadambari, one of the world's first novels, and the biography Harshacharita. Xuanzang, a Chinese pilgrim, travelled in India from 630 to 644, seeking Buddhist sites and teachers and taking back more than 600 manuscripts. Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj in his honour and every five years an assembly at Prayaga where he gave away wealth. Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha south of the Narmada.
concepts.example: Harsha's copper plate inscription reads 'By my own hand, the great king of kings, Shri Harsha'.

Harsha ruled from
questions.a: Kannauj

questions.a: To visit Buddhist sites and learn from teachers

questions.a: He was a poet and dramatist who wrote plays and a patron of scholars like Bana.

questions.a: Sthaneshvara (Thanesar)

questions.q: Xuanzang took back to China more than
questions.a: 600 manuscripts

questions.q: Why do historians use Harsha's plays and Bana's books even though they are stories?
questions.a: They reveal details of culture and society, such as governance, diversity, technology, food and clothing.

questions.q: What did Xuanzang say of Harsha and Kannauj?
questions.a: He described Kannauj as beautiful and prosperous and Harsha as a just and energetic ruler with a vast army, often on campaigns.

questions.q: Harsha showed broad-mindedness by
questions.a: respecting all schools of thought while being a Shiva devotee and attached to Buddhism
o: respecting all schools of thought while being a Shiva devotee and attached to Buddhism

questions.q: Explain how Harsha's empire was limited.
questions.a: Its extent is not known with certainty, he was stopped by Pulakeshin II in the south and conflicts with neighbours continued despite an alliance with Kamarupa.

questions.q: Why does the chapter compare Xuanzang with Faxian?
questions.a: Both were Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who left valuable accounts
o: Both were Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who left valuable accounts

questions.q: Compare Harsha's Prayaga gift-giving with an earlier ceremony from Part 1.
questions.a: It resembles the gift-giving of rulers such as Ashoka or the Guptas' donations, where wealth was distributed to religious groups and the poor.

questions.q: Explain the importance of Xuanzang's travelogue for historians.
questions.a: It records politics, diplomacy, culture and religion in the kingdoms he crossed and is a major source for the period.

questions.q: Was Harsha a great emperor? Give evidence for and against.
questions.a: For: patron of literature and just ruler; against: mixed success in uniting the north and stopped in the south. A reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Write a short diary entry of Xuanzang attending the assembly at Kannauj.
questions.a: An entry describing the city, kings and leaders of sects at the assembly and Harsha's welcome.

concepts.name: The Tripartite Struggle and the Palas
concepts.description: The struggle for Kannauj among the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas and the rise of the Pala dynasty and its universities.
concepts.idea: Three powers fought over Kannauj, and the Palas of Bengal patronised great monasteries.
concepts.rule: After Harsha died in 647 Kannauj became the centre of a long, indecisive Tripartite Struggle among the Palas from the east, the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan during the 8th and 9th centuries. In 750 CE the people chose Gopala to restore stability in Bengal; he founded the Pala dynasty. Dharmapala expanded the empire and patronised Mahayana Buddhism, founding Vikramashila in Bihar and Somapura in Bangladesh, and continued patronising Nalanda. Vikramashila had six colleges, about 3,000 scholars, and dvarapanditas who tested applicants; it was known for ties with Tibet. It was plundered by Bakhtiyar Khilji in the 12th century. Pala prosperity came from trade and eastern seaports.
concepts.example: Each college of Vikramashila had a 'scholar gatekeeper'.

questions.q: The first Pala king, chosen by the people in 750 CE, was ____.
questions.a: Gopala

questions.a: Kannauj

questions.a: Vikramashila

questions.q: Vikramashila stayed a great centre of learning for more than
questions.a: four centuries

questions.q: What was the Tripartite Struggle?
questions.a: A long indecisive war among three powers for Kannauj
o: A long indecisive war among three powers for Kannauj

questions.q: A dvarapandita was a scholar ____ who tested students.
questions.a: gatekeeper

questions.q: Why did Vikramashila have gatekeepers?
questions.a: Admission was highly selective

questions.q: How did the Pala empire become prosperous?
questions.a: Internal trade and maritime trade through eastern seaports
o: Internal trade and maritime trade through eastern seaports

questions.q: Name the three powers of the Tripartite Struggle and where they came from.
questions.a: The Palas from the east, the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan.

questions.q: Somapura monastery is in present-day
questions.a: Bangladesh

questions.q: Vikramashila was destroyed by
questions.a: Bakhtiyar Khilji

questions.q: Why was Kannauj so attractive to powerful dynasties?
questions.a: It lay in the Gangetic plains, a rich and central region controlling routes, so holding it meant power over north India.

questions.q: List two subjects studied at Vikramashila.
questions.a: Grammar, logic, Hindu and Buddhist philosophy, learning and rituals.

questions.q: Ancient monasteries such as Nalanda served as
questions.a: the universities of their time

questions.q: Explain how Pala rulers showed religious flexibility.
questions.a: Dharmapala patronised Buddhist learning while some successors, though patronising Buddhist institutions, were devotees of Shiva, showing fluid belief systems.

questions.q: Why was the struggle 'indecisive'?
questions.a: No power won lasting victory

questions.q: Compare Vikramashila and Nalanda.
questions.a: Both were great Buddhist centres of learning; Vikramashila was founded by Dharmapala with a strong Tibetan link, while Nalanda was older and was patronised by Harsha and the Palas.

questions.q: Explain why the Palas left a lasting legacy.
questions.a: They gave strong governance and learning through great monasteries and trade in eastern and northern India.

questions.q: Was choosing Gopala by the people a good way to select a ruler? Give reasons.
questions.a: It restored stability after disorder and shows popular support; a reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Design a prospectus page for Vikramashila with three features.
questions.a: A page listing six colleges, a vast library, subjects and the gatekeeper test.

concepts.name: The Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas
concepts.description: Nagabhata I and Bhoja of the Pratiharas, Dantidurga, Krishna I, Kailashanatha temple and Amoghavarsha.
concepts.idea: The Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas were major powers who built empires and great monuments.
concepts.rule: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, founded in the mid-8th century by Nagabhata I, probably came from western India (Gurjara was the region between Gujarat and Rajasthan). Bhoja, a Vishnu devotee, built an empire from Punjab and Saurashtra to Kannauj. The empire suffered when Rashtrakutas destroyed Kannauj and was finally ended by the Ghaznavids in the early 11th century. The Rashtrakutas began when Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas in the mid-8th century; the capital was Manyakheta (Malkheda) in Karnataka. Krishna I built the Kailashanatha temple at Ellora, the largest rock-cut temple in India, carved out of a hillside. Amoghavarsha I, called Nripatunga, reigned 64 years, was drawn to Jainism and wrote in Sanskrit and Kannada. Al-Masudi praised a Rashtrakuta ruler for honouring Islam.
concepts.example: The Kailashanatha temple is not a construction but a gigantic sculpture.

questions.a: It is carved out of a hillside like a gigantic sculpture
o: It is carved out of a hillside like a gigantic sculpture

questions.a: kings

questions.a: Vishnu

questions.a: They patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools equally
o: They patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools equally

questions.q: Name two achievements of the Rashtrakutas.
questions.a: The Kailashanatha temple, patronage of Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada, and temporary occupation of Kannauj.

questions.q: The Pratiharas were finally eliminated by the
questions.a: Ghaznavids

questions.q: 'Nrupatunga Road' in Bengaluru is named after
questions.a: Amoghavarsha I

questions.q: What did Al-Masudi's account say about a Rashtrakuta ruler?
questions.a: He praised the ruler, saying Islam was honoured and protected in his kingdom and mosques were built.

questions.q: Describe Bhoja's empire.
questions.a: It stretched from Punjab and Saurashtra in the west to Kannauj in the east, controlling most of north India.

questions.q: The Rashtrakutas were once
questions.a: subordinates (samantas) of the Chalukyas

questions.q: Explain why kings of these dynasties were not constantly at war.
questions.a: They also found time and resources to build wonders such as Ellora, patronise learning and ensure peace, as Amoghavarsha did.

questions.q: What does Al-Masudi's praise suggest?
questions.a: Rashtrakutas were tolerant of other faiths
o: Rashtrakutas were tolerant of other faiths

questions.q: Compare the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas.
questions.a: The Pratiharas came from western India and held Kannauj with Bhoja, while the Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan from Manyakheta and briefly occupied Kannauj.

questions.q: Explain how the fall of Kannauj affected the Pratiharas.
questions.a: The destruction of Kannauj by the Rashtrakutas hastened the disintegration of their empire, which the Ghaznavids finally ended.

questions.q: Which is more impressive, Amoghavarsha's reign or the Kailash temple? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned choice: a long peaceful reign gave stability, while the temple shows artistic achievement.

questions.q: Write a museum label for the Kailashanatha temple.
questions.a: A label with location Ellora, builder Krishna I, carving from a hillside and its size.

concepts.name: Kashmir, Kalhana and Shankaracharya
concepts.description: Kashmir's dynasties, Kalhana's Rajatarangini and historical method, and Adi Shankaracharya and Kashmir Shaivism.
concepts.idea: Kashmir was a centre of learning, and Kalhana set high standards for writing history.
concepts.rule: In the mid-8th century a new power arose in Kashmir. We know its rulers from Kalhana's Rajatarangini, the 'River of Kings', composed in the 12th century. Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty was a firm ruler; later Queen Didda consolidated power in the 10th century through alliances and by eliminating rivals. Kalhana said he examined eleven earlier chronicles and consulted inscriptions and grants, and that a good poet's words, like a judge's, should be free from love or hatred. Adi Shankaracharya of the 8th century taught advaita vedanta, that brahman is ultimate reality and the world is maya, and set up four mathas at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri. Kashmir Shaivism produced Abhinavagupta. Kashmir bridged Buddhist scholarship to Tibet and Central Asia.
concepts.example: The Shankaracharya temple stands on a hill overlooking the Kashmir valley near Srinagar.

questions.q: Kalhana wrote the ____, meaning the River of Kings.
questions.a: Rajatarangini

questions.a: Karkota dynasty

questions.a: four

questions.q: A great scholar of Kashmir Shaivism was
questions.a: Abhinavagupta

questions.a: free from love or hatred

questions.a: maya

questions.q: Kalhana gathered information from
questions.a: earlier chronicles and inscriptions

questions.q: Why is Kashmir called a bridge for Buddhist scholarship?
questions.a: Scholars and texts travelled between northern India, Tibet and Central Asia via Kashmir
o: Scholars and texts travelled between northern India, Tibet and Central Asia via Kashmir

questions.q: What did Shankaracharya teach about brahman?
questions.a: That brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness and the world is maya or illusion.

questions.q: Which city has a Shankaracharya matha?
questions.a: Puri

questions.q: The Rajatarangini was composed in the
questions.a: 12th century

questions.q: Name four cities where Shankaracharya set up mathas and suggest why in four corners.
questions.a: Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri; they are in the four corners of India so that his teaching would spread across the country.

questions.q: How did Kalhana overcome difficulties in writing history?
questions.a: He examined eleven earlier works and used inscriptions on temples, royal grants and other writings to correct errors.

questions.q: Queen Didda gained power through
questions.a: alliances and eliminating rivals

questions.q: Compare Kalhana's method with how history is written today.
questions.a: Like modern historians he used earlier works and inscriptions and tried to be impartial; today we use many more sources, archaeology and scientific dating.

questions.q: Why does Kalhana's condition make a historian more reliable?
questions.a: Being free from love or hatred avoids bias
o: Being free from love or hatred avoids bias

questions.q: Compare Shankaracharya's advaita with Kashmir Shaivism as traditions.
questions.a: Advaita vedanta stresses brahman as the ultimate reality and the world as maya, while Kashmir Shaivism was a Shaiva school with scholars like Abhinavagupta writing on philosophy, poetry and aesthetics.

questions.q: Explain how Kashmir was closely linked with the rest of the subcontinent.
questions.a: It was a centre of Sanskrit learning, its artisans and scholars were in demand across north India and it linked Buddhist scholarship to Tibet and Central Asia.

questions.q: Should historians be free from love or hatred? Discuss with an example.
questions.a: Yes, to be fair; but complete neutrality is hard, so we compare sources. A reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Draw a map placing Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri and describe their positions.
questions.a: A map showing Badrinath in the north, Puri in the east, Dwarka in the west and Sringeri in the south.

concepts.name: The Chalukyas and the Pallavas
concepts.description: Pulakeshin II, Badami and Aihole, the Eastern and Western Chalukyas, and the Pallavas of Kanchi and Mamallapuram.
concepts.idea: The Chalukyas of the Deccan and the Pallavas of the south rivalled each other and built great temples.
concepts.rule: Pulakeshin I founded the Chalukya dynasty in the mid-6th century. His grandson Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha's southward advance. The capital was Vatapi (Badami), famous for cave temples; Aihole has over a hundred temples and the Meguti Jain temple carries Ravikirti's long inscription praising Pulakeshin II, which exaggerates. Pulakeshin II was defeated by the Pallavas of Kanchi. The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi. The Pallavas peaked in the 7th century under Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla, who defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Badami. Kanchipuram was a cultural and economic hub. Mamallapuram, a seaport with Chinese, Persian and Roman coins, has the Shore Temple. Poet Dandin lived under the Pallavas. They fell to Chola king Aditya I.
concepts.example: Xuanzang visited both the Chalukya kingdom and Kanchi.

questions.a: Badami

questions.a: It is exaggerated and contradicted by other inscriptions

o: an unwritten boundary between the Pallavas and Chalukyas

questions.q: Why do coins from China, Persia and Rome at Mamallapuram matter?

questions.q: What did Xuanzang say about Kanchi?

questions.q: In the early 7th century the two great powers of India were
questions.a: Harsha in the north and Pulakeshin II in the south

questions.q: Explain the rivalry between the Chalukyas and the Pallavas.
questions.a: Pulakeshin II expanded the Chalukya kingdom but was defeated by the Pallavas, and Narasimhavarman I captured Badami before retreating to the Tungabhadra.

questions.q: Why is Kanchipuram called an economic hub?
questions.a: It traded in spices, textiles, silk and ivory
o: It traded in spices, textiles, silk and ivory

questions.q: Compare the Chalukyas of Badami with the Eastern Chalukyas.
questions.a: Badami Chalukyas were the main dynasty of the Deccan; the Eastern branch ruled from Vengi, clashed with the Rashtrakutas and promoted Telugu and Kannada literature.

questions.q: Explain how both dynasties contributed to art and literature.
questions.a: The Chalukyas built cave temples at Badami and Aihole while the Pallavas built temples and rock-cut caves at Mamallapuram and patronised Sanskrit and Tamil poets like Dandin.

questions.q: Who was the more successful, Pulakeshin II or Narasimhavarman I? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned answer: Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha but lost to the Pallavas, who captured Badami.

concepts.name: The Pandyas, Cheras and Cholas
concepts.description: The southern kingdoms of the period, and the rise of the Cholas under Vijayalaya and Aditya I.
concepts.idea: The Pandyas, Cheras and Cholas re-emerged, and the Cholas built a great empire.
concepts.rule: The Pandya, Chola and Chera kingdoms were mentioned in Ashoka's edict and Sangam literature and re-emerged. The Pandyas rose by the 6th century, allied with the Chalukyas and Pallavas, controlled southern Tamil Nadu, traded with Southeast Asia through Korkai and had Madurai as capital; they translated the Mahabharata into Tamil, which has not survived. In the 10th century the Cholas swept them aside. The Cheras (Chera Perumals) kept independence on the Kerala coast. The Cholas were reborn under Vijayalaya in the 9th century with capital at Thanjavur; his son Aditya I defeated the Pallavas. The Cholas built one of the largest empires in the south, known for efficient administration, a powerful navy, grand temples and use of Tamil and Sanskrit; the Kaveri delta and irrigation ensured prosperity. Inscriptions used Sanskrit for praise and the local language for details.
concepts.example: An early Chola bronze of Nataraja symbolises the dance of creation and destruction.

questions.q: How did the Pandyas' alliances shape the South?

questions.q: What does the Chola use of both Tamil and Sanskrit show?

questions.q: Why did the Cheras keep their independence?

questions.q: Compare the Pandyas and the Cholas.

questions.q: Explain the role of irrigation in the Chola empire.

questions.q: Which southern kingdom achieved most? Justify.

concepts.name: Polity, economy and society in the period
concepts.description: Samantas and decentralised kingdoms, administration, land grants, trade, guilds, jatis, women and queens.
concepts.idea: Kingdoms were decentralised, land grants grew, trade linked far markets and society grew more complex.
concepts.rule: With the fall of large empires, smaller decentralised kingdoms arose. Kings ruled core regions directly and other regions through samantas, tributaries who led armies and managed local administration but whose loyalty could be fragile; the Rashtrakutas, once samantas of the Chalukyas, overthrew them. Territory was divided into provinces (bhuktis or rashtras), districts (mandalas) and villages, which were largely self-governed. The land grant system expanded, creating a class of landholders. The Pallavas built many tanks still working today. Small traders, ship-owning merchants and guilds thrived. Jatis multiplied; the Palas and Kakatiyas were originally Shudras. The Kayasthas became a jati in the 10th century. Discrimination is seen in terms like asprishya. Queen Tribhuvana Mahadevi I ruled the Bhauma-Karas in the 9th century.
concepts.example: Xuanzang described butchers, fishers and scavengers living outside the city.

o: They led armies and managed local administration

questions.a: Iran, Iraq and east Africa

questions.q: Why could samantas be a danger to kings?
questions.a: Their loyalty was fragile when central authority weakened and some grew strong enough to overthrow overlords, as the Rashtrakutas did.

questions.q: Give two examples of women's roles in the period.
questions.a: Bana showed women working in agriculture, crafts and courts as musicians and storytellers, and inscriptions record women making offerings and building water structures; queens also ruled.

questions.q: Copper plates mention traders from West Asia who were

questions.q: Explain both the positive and negative sides of the jati system in this period.
questions.a: Jatis and varnas cooperated economically and were flexible, but discrimination against groups regarded as impure, such as asprishya, existed.

questions.q: Why was urban decline an oversimplified view?
questions.a: Many older cities remained and new ones emerged
o: Many older cities remained and new ones emerged

questions.q: Compare direct rule and rule through samantas.
questions.a: Direct rule was in core regions with provinces and officials; rule through samantas governed other regions via tributary chiefs.

questions.q: Explain how trade and temples supported cities in the south.
questions.a: Temples acted as centres of commerce and ports fuelled maritime trade, so cities flourished as political, economic and religious hubs.

questions.q: Were decentralised kingdoms better than large empires? Give reasons.
questions.a: A reasoned answer weighing local self-government and stability against constant rivalry.

questions.q: Draw a chart of an administrative hierarchy from king to village with officials.
questions.a: A chart showing king, provinces, districts, villages with headmen, accountants and committees.

concepts.name: Religion, bhakti, and science and mathematics
concepts.description: Pluralism among religions, Tantra, Jainism, the Puranas, the Alvars and Nayanars, and mathematicians such as Brahmagupta.
concepts.idea: Rulers patronised many faiths, bhakti spread across India, and Indian mathematics flourished.
concepts.rule: Rulers generally patronised Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, which coexisted peacefully mostly. Tantric schools emerged around the 6th century. Buddhism declined outside the east as temple-based Hinduism and bhakti rose; Jainism remained popular in western India and Karnataka, with the monolithic Bahubali at Shravanabelagola. The Puranas integrated local deities into pan-Indian cults. Bhakti spread from the south through the 12 Alvars, devotees of Vishnu including Andal, and 63 Nayanars, devotees of Shiva, writing in Tamil; bhakti was open to all across gender and social divisions. Brahmagupta, born in 598 CE in Bhillamala, wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta with rules for zero, negative numbers and fractions. Bhaskara I worked on trigonometry, Virahanka on the sequence later called Fibonacci, and Mahavira wrote the first maths text independent of astronomy.
concepts.example: Arab scholars adopted the Indian decimal system with zero, later called 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.

questions.q: State two features of the Bhakti movement.
questions.a: It emerged from diverse social backgrounds, used regional languages and invoked a direct personal relationship with the divine, cutting across gender and social divisions.

questions.q: How did Indian numerals reach Europe?
questions.a: Arabs translated Sanskrit texts and adopted the decimal system with zero, then transmitted it to Europe where it was called Arabic numerals.

questions.q: Why did mathematicians of this period refine astronomy?
questions.a: They wanted reliable calendars and precise predictions of eclipses and planet positions.

questions.q: Explain how kings' patronage helped science and art.
questions.a: Royal support funded scholars, temples and astronomy, so long knowledge traditions could continue across centuries.

questions.q: Why did Buddhism decline outside the east?
questions.a: Temple-based Hinduism and bhakti rose

questions.q: Compare Alvars and Nayanars.
questions.a: Alvars were 12 devotees of Vishnu including Andal, and Nayanars were 63 devotees of Shiva including three women; both composed Tamil devotional poetry.

questions.q: Explain how bhakti reshaped Indian society and literature.
questions.a: By using regional languages and offering direct devotion open to all, it cut across social divisions and inspired literature whose impact lingers.

questions.q: Which contribution, bhakti or mathematics, has a greater lasting impact? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned choice: bhakti shaped society and literature, while mathematics gave the number system to the world.

concepts.name: Foreign invasions: the Hunas and the Arabs
concepts.description: The Huna invasions and assimilation, the Arab arrival, Muhammad bin Qasim, resistance and cultural exchanges with Arabia.
concepts.idea: The Hunas were assimilated, while the Arabs' conquest in India was limited and cultural exchange flourished.
concepts.rule: The Huns were nomads from Central Asia who overran much of Europe; the Hunas of Indian sources weakened the Guptas and in the early 6th century pushed into the Ganga plains until the Aulikara kings of Dashapura (Mandsaur), including Yashodharma, defeated them. By the 7th century the Hunas had assimilated, adopting Sanskrit, Gupta-style titles and coin designs. Arab naval raids in 637 hit Thana, Bharuch and Debal without lasting control. Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, killing King Dahar at Aror. Indian chiefs regained most of it within two years. Nagabhata I of the Pratiharas and Lalitaditya of Kashmir resisted Arab advances. Arab dominion was limited to two small states in Sindh and Punjab. Trade with Arabia was old; the word monsoon comes from mawsim. Sanskrit texts of mathematics, astronomy and medicine were translated into Arabic in the 9th century.
concepts.example: Sandalwood, camphor and pepper have words in Sanskrit and Arabic with similar sounds.

questions.a: Nagabhata I of the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Lalitaditya Muktapida of Kashmir.

questions.a: Arabs

questions.q: How did the Hunas show assimilation in India?
questions.a: They served as soldiers and in local administration, adopted Sanskrit and Prakrit and used Gupta-style titles, coins and religious symbols.

questions.q: Why did Arab gains in India remain limited?
questions.a: Indian rulers offered stubborn resistance and sometimes formed alliances, so Arab rule survived only in two small states in Sindh and Punjab.

questions.q: Which shows old trade links between India and Arabia?
questions.a: ships sailing with monsoon winds long before Islam
o: ships sailing with monsoon winds long before Islam

questions.q: Compare the Huna and Arab invasions in aims, methods and impact.
questions.a: The Hunas were nomadic raiders who weakened the Guptas and then assimilated; the Arabs came with a religious motive and armies, conquered Sindh but had limited impact and did not spread beyond.

questions.q: Why did Al-Istakhri say Arab dominion was limited?
questions.a: After three centuries only two petty states remained
o: After three centuries only two petty states remained

questions.q: Compare the reaction of India to the Hunas and to the Arabs.
questions.a: The Hunas were defeated and assimilated, while the Arabs were resisted for a long time and limited to Sindh and Punjab.

questions.q: Explain the importance of cultural exchange between India and Arabia.
questions.a: Sanskrit works on mathematics, astronomy and medicine were translated into Arabic and India's numerals spread to Europe; words like sandal and camphor also passed.

questions.q: Did India show resilience against foreign invasions? Justify.
questions.a: Yes, rulers defeated the Hunas and resisted the Arabs and absorbed foreign groups; a reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Create a table of foreign groups in Indian history from Part I and II with when they came and what happened.
questions.a: A table with Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas, Hunas and Arabs with dates and outcomes such as assimilation or limited conquest.
